extracted.intended_audience: Victorian readers, novelists (especially women), and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria for judging 'lady novelists' (Victorian women novelists), identifying stylistic, moral, and realistic failures such as affectation, oracular preaching, false erudition, and heterogeneous sensational incidents. The page both diagnoses common faults and illustrates them with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude in high society but failure elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Verisimilitude in their representations of the high society in which they seem to live; but then they betray no closer acquaintance with any other form of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may render fashionable society plausibly yet show no acquaintance with other social milieus: literary men, tradespeople, and cottagers become 'impossible.' Example contrast: credible peers vs impossible cottagers; criticism: breadth of observation is required, not only familiar social circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic child-speech
rubrics_metrics.description: There are few women...who have not seen something of children under five years of age, yet...we have a child of four and a half years old talking in this Ossianic fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children's dialogue should match their age and experience; the anti-pattern is a precocious, poetical child speaking like an adult to convey sentiment or profundity (example quoted at length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible talents and erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroine can pick up Oriental tongues...with the same aërial facility that the butterfly sips nectar...she can talk with perfect correctness in any language, except English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't bestow implausible, encyclopaedic accomplishments on heroines for effect. Avoid the trope of the unrealistically polyglot/genius heroine whose learning serves only to dazzle rather than to be credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous display of classical learning in inappropriate contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is as little the custom of well-bred men as of well-bred women to quote Latin in mixed parties; they can contain their familiarity with 'the humane Cicero' without allowing it to boil over in ordinary conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Latin or classical authors in casual mixed-company scenes feels inauthentic and is an affectation; authors should match register and occasion when showing erudition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inopportune long-windedness
rubrics_metrics.description: We have often met with women much more novel and profound in their observations than Laura Gay, but rarely with any so inopportunely long-winded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving characters or narrators unnecessarily long rhetorical or philosophical speeches that break narrative plausibility; verbosity that interrupts action undermines credibility (example: Laura Gay's long philosophical passage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on sensational, heterogeneous incidents (pot-pourri plotting)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a wonderful pot pourri of Almack’s, Scotch second-sight, Mr. Rogers’s breakfasts, Italian brigands, death-bed conversions, superior authoresses, Italian mistresses, and attempts at poisoning old ladies...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assemble exotic or sensational elements merely because each is 'pretty' — mixing unrelated romantic tropes produces an incoherent patchwork rather than an organic plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affected diction and stylistic inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: The colloquial style of these novels is often marked by much ingenious inversion, and a careful avoidance of such cheap phraseology as can be heard every day...minds are redolent of various things; hearts are hollow; events are utilized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mannered inversions and over-wrought locutions that substitute novelty of phrase for genuine expression of character or feeling; beware of stock phrases like 'minds are redolent' that feel artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using novels as vehicles for oracular dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: The oracular species—novels intended to expound the writer’s religious, philosophical, or moral theories...she is ready to remedy their omission by setting before you a complete theory of life and manual of divinity in a love story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction should not be merely a sermon or manual of divinity. When plot and character are subordinated to doctrinal exposition, the work becomes unrealistic and pedantic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking vagueness for depth and bombast for eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: She mistakes vagueness for depth, bombast for eloquence, and affectation for originality; she struts on one page, rolls her eyes on another, grimaces in a third, and is hysterical in a fourth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute clear insight for rhetorical fog; avoid grandiose language that masks lack of substance—readers mark such passages as empty posturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: False picture of the visible while expounding the invisible
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of a lady novelist to describe actual life and her fellow-men is in inverse proportion to her confident eloquence about God and the other world...the means by which she usually chooses to conduct you to true ideas of the invisible is a totally false picture of the visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a novelist aims to convey spiritual or philosophical truths, the depiction of ordinary life must remain truthful; do not distort everyday reality to force doctrinal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandiloquent periphrasis for commonplace objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonplace people would say that a copy of Shakespeare lay on a drawing-room table; but the authoress...tells you that there lay on the table, 'that fund of human thought and feeling, which teaches the heart through the little name, 'Shakespeare.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use inflated circumlocutions to make ordinary objects sound portentous; prefer clear, direct description unless a deliberate stylistic purpose justifies ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confused metaphors and obscurantism
rubrics_metrics.description: You see clearly, of course, how colors are first engraven on the soul, and then blent into the wide arch...on which arch of colors—apparently a rainbow—the law of order grew and multiplied, each—apparently the arch and the law—perfect after his kind?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tangled metaphors that obscure meaning; clarity should not be sacrificed to loftiness. The passage is given as an example of metaphors so confused they defeat comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-dramatization/melodramatic treatment of trivial events
rubrics_metrics.description: Very ordinary events of civilized life are exalted into the most awful crises, and ladies in full skirts...conduct themselves not unlike the heroines of sanguinary melodramas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve melodramatic intensity for truly dramatic moments; turning household misunderstandings into stage-like crises strains plausibility and fatigues the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incoherent assemblage of exotic characters and improbable revelations
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a blind Irish harper...a crazy gypsy...a dwarfish miserly merchant...and we have an ultra-virtuous Irish Barney...revealing secret on her death-bed which...goes to prove that Ernest...is Kate’s brother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting stereotypical or exotic figures solely to contrive sensational revelations (e.g., deathbed confessions proving kinship). Such devices indicate fabrication rather than organic plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical emphasis as substitute for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The italics and small caps are the author's, and we hope they assist the reader’s comprehension...the style is quite as lofty as its purpose; indeed, some passages on which we have spent much patient study are quite beyond our reach, in spite of the illustrative aid of italics and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on italics, small caps, or typographic tricks to signify profundity; they cannot fix muddled thought and often highlight obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper choice of milieu for the novel's theme
rubrics_metrics.description: The real drama of Evangelicalism...lies among the middle and lower classes...Why, then, cannot our Evangelical lady novelists show us the operation of their religious views among people...who keep no carriage...instead of seeking subjects among titles and carriages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set thematic material in the social context where it naturally belongs. If a doctrine concerns the lower classes, depicting it only in aristocratic drawing-rooms rings false and wastes dramatic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snobbishness and class bias in moralizing fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Evangelical silliness is as snobbish as any other kind of silliness...pious ladies nauseate us with novels which remind us of what we sometimes see in a worldly woman recently 'converted'...she is as fond of a fine dinner-table as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid marrying moral or religious themes to snobbish portrayals of society. Moralizing that comforts or flatters the fashionable classes is suspect; authenticity requires attention to class realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagey, theatrical tableaux and exaggerated postures
rubrics_metrics.description: Happening one day to see Horace talking to Grace at a window...she suddenly rushes up to them and clasps them both, saying, 'with a flushed countenance and in an excited manner'...Gathering herself up to an unprecedented height (!) her eyes lightening forth the fire of her anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid directions and theatrical set-pieces masquerading as narrative description; characters should act and speak plausibly rather than striking 'tableaux' poses for melodramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of genuine social observation leading to caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is less excusable in an Evangelical novelist than in any other, gratuitously to seek her subjects among titles and carriages...the authoress's questionable English would be strictly consistent [among working classes].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should have real acquaintance with the social groups they depict; inventing stereotyped manners or language for convenience results in caricature rather than understanding.
